headline: Common Bathroom Plumbing Mistakes to Avoid During Your Remodel
articleBody:
Remodeling your bathroom is a fantastic way to update your home, but the plumbing part can be tricky. It’s easy to make small errors that turn into big, wet problems if you’re not careful. You want your new bathroom to be a source of relaxation, not frustration, so here are some common plumbing mistakes we see and how to sidestep them during your remodel.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Failing to shut off and verify the water supply: This might sound basic, but forgetting to fully shut off the main water supply (or the specific fixture’s shutoff) before disconnecting pipes is a surefire way to cause a flood. Even worse is assuming it's off when it isn't.

How to avoid it: Always test the faucet after turning off the water to confirm it’s completely off before loosening any connections. If you can’t locate or access your main shutoff, or if it doesn’t work, get a professional involved right away.

Disconnecting the trap without containing residual water: The P-trap under your sink always holds a bit of water to block sewer gases. If you just unhook it, you’ll have a messy puddle (and potentially smelly water) on your floor.

How to avoid it: Keep a bucket or towel handy directly under the P-trap when you’re disconnecting it to catch any water.

Forcing mismatched fittings: Plumbing connections need to be precise. Trying to force fittings that don't match exactly can strip threads, crack pipes, and lead to immediate or future leaks. It's often tempting to make something 'just fit'.

How to avoid it: Always use fittings of the correct size and material. If a connection doesn't feel right, stop and verify you have the proper components. Don't underestimate the importance of snug, but not overly tight, connections.

Positioning pipes where cabinet drawers or shelves will interfere: This is a classic remodel mistake! You install your beautiful new vanity, only to find the drain pipe runs right through where a drawer or shelf should be, rendering it useless.

How to avoid it: Before securing any pipes within the wall or cabinet, dry-fit your vanity and mark the exact locations of drawers and shelves. Adjust your pipe rough-ins accordingly to ensure full functionality of your cabinet storage.

Failing to perform a thorough leak test after reassembly: Rushing to finish and skipping the leak test is a recipe for disaster. Even small drips can cause significant damage over time.

How to avoid it: After reconnecting all plumbing, gradually turn the water back on. Run the faucet, flush the toilet, and check *every single connection* for drips, not just once, but over several minutes. Look for even tiny beads of water.
